titre: The Mirror Box That Calms a Phantom Limb
accroche: A mirror placed in front of an intact hand is enough, in several amputees tested in 1996, to make a painful phantom limb move or disappear.
contenu_vulgarise:
After an amputation, the missing limb does not always disappear from perception. Many patients go on feeling it, sometimes frozen in a clenched, painful position, with no voluntary movement able to make it budge: there is no longer a limb to send the command to. In the 1990s, the neurologist Vilayanur Ramachandran proposes a deliberately rudimentary device to tackle this paradox, a box open at the top, fitted in its center with a vertical mirror.

## A Reflection in Place of the Missing Limb

The patient slides the intact limb to one side of the mirror, and the stump to the other, so that the reflection of the intact limb visually occupies the spot where the brain places the phantom limb. By moving the intact hand or arm while watching this reflection, some patients then report what no mental exercise had managed to produce: the phantom limb, too, seems to move.

Ramachandran and Diane Rogers-Ramachandran test the device on ten amputees, in a study published in 1996. Six of them feel a kinesthetic movement of the phantom limb in the presence of the mirror. In four patients suffering from painful spasms, the box brings relief. One patient, after repeated practice, sees his phantom arm simply disappear. Three or four also report a form of tactile synesthesia: a touch on the reflected hand is felt, literally, on the absent hand.

## Recalibrating a Map, Not Repairing a Nerve

The brain constantly maintains a map of the body, fed at once by proprioception, touch, and vision. After an amputation, this map keeps representing a limb that no longer sends any signal, and can freeze at its last known position. The mirror acts on no severed nerve: it supplies visual evidence, which the brain accepts as reliable enough to update the map, even though the real proprioceptive information has been gone since the amputation. Ramachandran notes that this reorganization can set in within less than three weeks of practice.

The idea has since left the laboratory: mirror therapy is now among the treatments offered for phantom limb pain. A systematic review published in 2024 concludes that pain is genuinely reduced, while noting that the available evidence remains, for now, of limited quality: a gap between a widely confirmed clinical intuition and controlled trials still too few to demonstrate it without reservation.

repere.texte: Of ten amputees tested with the mirror box, six felt a movement of the phantom limb, four had their painful spasms relieved, and one saw his phantom arm disappear after repeated practice.
repere.source: Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 263(1369), 1996

carte.punch: A simple mirror made painful phantom limbs move, and sometimes disappear.
carte.idee: In the 1990s, Vilayanur Ramachandran places a mirror in front of an amputee's intact hand, at the spot of the phantom limb. The reflection is enough, in several patients tested in 1996, to unlock a frozen limb, even to ease a pain that no voluntary movement could reach.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: An overview of later clinical uses, beyond the phantom limb.

quiz.question: Why can the reflection of an intact limb, seen in a mirror, relieve the pain felt in an amputated limb?
choix: Because the mirror locally anesthetizes the nerve endings of the stump
Because the mirror directly stimulates the motor areas of the cortex through an optical reflex
Because staring at a reflection simply diverts the patient's attention from the pain
Because the reflection gives the brain visual evidence with which to recalibrate its body map, frozen since the amputation
quiz.explication: The mirror acts neither on the nerves of the stump nor directly on the motor cortex, and the effect goes beyond a simple distraction: several patients report a movement, even a lasting disappearance of the phantom limb, not just a temporary respite. The brain maintains a body map updated by several senses at once; deprived of real proprioceptive information since the amputation, this map accepts the reflection as sufficient visual evidence to recalibrate itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many amputees did the 1996 study test, and how many felt their phantom limb move?
choix: Ten amputees tested, six felt a movement of the phantom
Ten amputees tested, all felt a movement of the phantom
One hundred amputees tested, a third felt a movement
Four amputees tested, only one felt a movement
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of the ten amputees tested by Ramachandran and Diane Rogers-Ramachandran, six felt a kinesthetic movement of the phantom limb in front of the mirror, four had their painful spasms relieved, and one saw his phantom arm disappear.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did three or four patients report, in addition to the movement?
choix: A diffuse warmth in the stump after each session
The immediate and permanent disappearance of all pain
A touch on the reflected hand felt on the absent hand
A visual discomfort that kept them from staring at the reflection for long
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is a form of tactile synesthesia: touching the reflected hand is felt, literally, on the hand that is no longer there. One patient did see his phantom arm disappear, but after repeated practice, not immediately.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2024 systematic review conclude about mirror therapy?
choix: That it brings no benefit beyond a simple distraction
That it genuinely reduces pain, on evidence of limited quality
That it has become the only recommended treatment in this area
That it works only within the three weeks following the amputation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The review concludes that pain is genuinely reduced, while noting that the available evidence remains of limited quality. The three weeks Ramachandran mentions are an observed reorganization time, not a window beyond which the mirror would stop working.
